Because that single buyer controls demand, it can push prices down and dictate terms, since sellers have nowhere else to go. A classic example is a company town where one employer hires all the labor, so it can set wages below what a competitive market would produce.

Think of entropy as how many ways you can rearrange the hidden details of a system and still have it look the same from the outside. A shuffled deck has high entropy because there are astronomically many orderings that all just look like "a shuffled deck." A deck sorted ace through king has low entropy, because almost any rearrangement would visibly break the pattern. So entropy isn't messiness itself, it's the count of arrangements that match what you can actually observe. More matching arrangements means higher entropy, and that's also why it measures how much you don't know about the fine details.

[[GIST]] entropy counts hidden arrangements that look identical

Start from a portfolio that's long one option and short delta units of the stock, so its value is Π = V − ΔS. Over a small step dt, the stock follows dS = μS dt + σS dW, and Ito's lemma gives dV = (∂V/∂t + μS ∂V/∂S + ½σ²S² ∂²V/∂S²) dt + σS ∂V/∂S dW. Pick Δ = ∂V/∂S so the dW terms cancel, leaving dΠ = (∂V/∂t + ½σ²S² ∂²V/∂S²) dt. That portfolio is now riskless, so it must earn the risk-free rate, dΠ = rΠ dt = r(V − S ∂V/∂S) dt. Setting the two equal and rearranging gives ∂V/∂t + ½σ²S² ∂²V/∂S² + rS ∂V/∂S − rV = 0.

The lecturer's right, and the correct reading is the other way round: a p-value is the probability of seeing data at least as extreme as yours, **assuming the null hypothesis is true**. So it's a statement about the data given the null, not about the null given the data. The spending multiplier is **5**. With an MPC of 0.8, each dollar of new spending gets re-spent as 80 cents, then 64 cents, and so on, and the sum of that chain is 1 divided by (1 minus 0.8), which is 1 over 0.2.

Because each round of spending is smaller than the last, and those rounds add up to a finite total. If I spend a dollar, the recipient spends 80 cents of it, the next person spends 80 percent of that, and so on. That's a geometric series: 1 + 0.8 + 0.8² + 0.8³ and so on. The sum of that series is 1 divided by (1 minus 0.8), which is 5. So the multiplier isn't a coincidence, it's just the total of all those shrinking rounds of re-spending.

[[GIST]] shrinking rounds sum to five

The theorem holds only when transaction costs are zero and bargaining is costless, which is why it's a benchmark rather than a description. Once you add real costs, who holds the right absolutely changes the outcome, because the party with the right starts from a different threat point and the surplus gets eaten by negotiation, enforcement, and holdout. So the useful move is to ask which specific friction is doing the work: information asymmetry, many parties, or the inability to write a complete contract. That's what tells you whether the right should sit with the polluter, the victim, or a regulator.

Because the theorem's assumptions are the opposite of how real bargaining works. Zero transaction costs means no cost to finding the other party, negotiating, writing the contract, or enforcing it, and that almost never holds. Add asymmetric information, so each side doesn't know the other's true costs and values, and large groups, where free-riding and holdouts block agreement, and the conditions collapse. So the efficient outcome is reachable in principle, but the assignment of the right still matters in practice.

[[GIST]] zero transaction costs almost never hold

The Lerner index check on Slide 16 works out like this. For tourists, (70 − 20)/70 = **0.714**, which means |Ed| = **1.4**. For commuters, (40 − 20)/40 = **0.5**, which means |Ed| = 2.

What the two numbers tell you: the Lerner index measures markup power, so the higher it is, the more market power the ferry has over that group. Tourists show a bigger markup and a lower elasticity, so they're the less price-sensitive group and get charged the higher price of 70. Commuters are more elastic, so their price is lower at 40. That's exactly the third-degree rule: the group with less elastic demand pays more.

[[GIST]] higher Lerner means less elastic, higher price

Right, that's the third condition doing all the work. Third-degree pricing only holds because the commuter fare can't leak to tourists. If resale is possible, commuters buy at 40 and undercut the ferry's 70, and the tourist price falls until the two meet. At that point the two groups are effectively one market, so the firm is back to charging a single price and the whole split collapses.

[[GIST]] no resale, or one price

Two things are going on. Taxes and imports are **leakages**: a slice of each extra dollar leaves the domestic spending chain before it gets re-spent, so less of it becomes someone else's income. Taxes go to the government, imports go abroad, and neither one comes back as the next round of domestic consumption, so the chain dies out faster and the multiplier shrinks.

Real-world estimates come in lower for the same reason, plus a few more. The simple formula assumes every dollar gets spent at the same rate forever, but in reality people save more of a windfall, some spending leaks into imports, and the economy is already near full capacity, so extra demand partly shows up as higher prices rather than more output. Crowding out and interest-rate rises work the same way.

With a 25 percent income tax, the effective MPC becomes 0.8 times 0.75, which is 0.6, so the multiplier is 1 divided by 0.4, which is **2.5**.

[[GIST]] leakages shrink the multiplier to 2.5

Tourists pay more because their demand is **less elastic**. At the profit-maximizing point, the Lerner index for tourists is 0.714, giving |Ed| = 1.4, while commuters sit at 0.5, giving |Ed| = 2. The rule is to set marginal revenue equal to the common marginal cost in each market, and the group that's less responsive to price ends up paying the higher price: 70 for tourists versus 40 for commuters.

Clock beat LRU on that string because Clock only approximates LRU, and on this particular reference string the approximation happened to evict better victims, landing on 7 faults against LRU's 8. The professor's point is that Clock is not always worse, just not always equal.

Real kernels don't do exact LRU because it needs a timestamp or list update on every single memory reference, and no real MMU provides that. It's too expensive in hardware.

Tern, the Lab 5 teaching kernel, uses Clock-style second chance, with a thrash monitor that suspends the process with the largest resident set when the system-wide fault rate exceeds 1 fault per 500 references for 3 consecutive sampling windows.

Clock is second chance: frames in a circle, one use bit each, set by hardware on every reference. On a fault the hand sweeps: use bit 1 means clear it and advance, use bit 0 means evict that page, load the new one, and set its bit to 1. A newly loaded page always starts with its use bit set.

For the slide 11 string, 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3 with 3 frames: fill frames 0, 1, 2 with 7, 0, 1, hand back at frame 0. Then 2 faults, the hand clears frame 0, clears frame 1, clears frame 2, comes back to frame 0 at 0 and evicts 7. The hand now sits at frame 1. The next 0 is a hit, so set frame 1's bit to 1. Then 3 faults and the hand sweeps from frame 1, clearing bits until it finds a 0. Keep going through 0, 4, 2, 3 and you land on 7 faults.

On the final, write the use bits and the hand position after every fault, since that's what's being graded.

[[GIST]] clock trace, use bits and hand

Here's how to trace Clock on the slide 11 string, 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3, with 3 frames.

Set up three empty frames in a circle, hand at frame 0, and a use bit per frame. Empty frames fill in order from frame 0, and a newly loaded page starts with its use bit set to 1. On a fault, the hand sweeps: if the use bit is 1, clear it and advance; if it's 0, evict that page and load the new one there. After any replacement, the hand points to the frame after the one you just filled.

Walking it: 7, 0, 1 fill frames 0, 1, 2, each with use bit 1. Then 2 faults, the hand sweeps past 7, 0, 1 clearing their bits, and evicts 7. Then 0 is a hit, so its use bit goes back to 1. Then 3 faults, the hand clears 0's bit and evicts 0. Then 0 faults again, the hand clears 1 and 2 and evicts 1. Then 4 faults, the hand clears 2 and evicts 2. Then 2 faults, the hand clears 3 and 0 and evicts 3. Then 3 faults, the hand clears 0 and 4 and evicts 0. That's 7 faults, matching the slide.

For the final, show the use bits and hand position after every fault, and remember Clock only approximates LRU on average, so it can beat LRU on a given string.

[[GIST]] clock trace, 7 faults on slide 11

A heap is optimized for one thing: getting the min or max in constant time, with insert and extract in O(log n). It's a partial order, so a parent is only guaranteed to beat its children, which is why you can't search it efficiently. A BST keeps a full ordering, so search, insert, and delete are all O(log n) and you can do ordered traversal, range queries, and find predecessors and successors. So if I need a priority queue, a heap. If I need ordered lookups or sorted iteration, a BST, and a balanced one like a red-black or AVL tree to keep that log n guarantee.

Quicksort goes quadratic when the pivot splits the array badly every time, like always picking the smallest or largest element, so each partition peels off one item and you get n levels of work instead of log n. Sorted or reverse-sorted input with a first-or-last pivot is the classic trigger. Real implementations avoid it by choosing the pivot better, median-of-three or a random element, and by switching to insertion sort on small subarrays. Introsort adds a depth counter and falls back to heapsort if recursion gets too deep, which guarantees O(n log n) worst case. Three-way partitioning also helps a lot when there are many duplicate keys.

[[GIST]] bad pivots cause quadratic, randomization and introsort fix it

Brute force is to fix each starting index i, walk j forward accumulating the running sum, and check after each step whether it equals k, keeping the longest j minus i plus 1 that matches. It's correct because every contiguous subarray is exactly some pair i, j, so checking all of them can't miss the answer. That's O(n²) time and O(1) extra space, and it's slow because for each of the n starts we rescan up to n elements.

The optimal approach is a prefix-sum hash map. Let prefix[i] be the sum of the first i elements. A subarray from i to j sums to k exactly when prefix[j+1] minus prefix[i] equals k, so for each position we look up whether prefix[j+1] minus k has been seen before, and if so the length is the current index minus that stored index. We store the earliest index for each prefix sum, and seed the map with 0 mapped to index minus one so subarrays starting at the beginning are handled. That's O(n) time and O(n) space.

A sliding window does not work here. The usual window trick relies on the sum being monotonic as you move the boundaries, which holds for non-negative numbers, but with negatives adding an element can decrease the sum and shrinking can increase it, so you can't decide whether to advance the right edge or the left edge. The prefix-sum map is what handles that.

[[GIST]] prefix-sum map beats sliding window with negatives

Sweep line with events. For each hold I make two events: a start at `start` with +1, and an end at `end` with -1. Sort all events by time, and at the same time process all the -1s before the +1s, so a hold ending at 40 and one starting at 40 don't count as overlapping. Then I walk the sorted events keeping a running count, and whenever the count beats the best so far, I record that time as the earliest instant the new max is reached. That's O(n log n) time and O(n) space, which fits the 200,000 limit.

I'd split it into three stages so each one is independently retryable. First, a snapshot stage that freezes the day's ledger entries into a settlement run with a run ID, so nothing downstream reads a moving table. Second, a per-grower aggregation stage that computes each payout from that frozen set, sharded by grower so it parallelizes and a single grower's failure doesn't take down the batch. Third, a submission stage that sends the bank file and records the acknowledgement.

For rerun safety, the whole thing keys on the run ID and is idempotent. Each grower's payout row is written with a unique key on run ID plus grower, so recomputing overwrites rather than double-pays. The bank submission carries an idempotency key per payout, and I only mark a payout as sent after the bank's ack comes back, so a crash mid-send means the rerun resends and the bank dedupes. I'd also make the run resumable: it tracks which shards completed, so a rerun picks up the unfinished ones instead of redoing everything.

What I page on is the things that threaten the deadline or the money. The batch not starting at 02:00, the run not finishing with enough buffer before banks open, any grower whose payout fails to reconcile against the ledger, and a bank submission that errors or never acks. Reconciliation mismatches page immediately because that's a correctness problem, not just a latency one.

[[GIST]] snapshot, aggregate, submit; idempotent reruns; page on deadline and reconciliation

I'd run a consensus layer, something like etcd or Patroni, as the source of truth for who's primary. Each node heartbeats to the leader; if the primary misses its lease, the leader marks it down and promotes the replica with the least replication lag, so we don't lose acknowledged writes. Clients never hardcode the primary, they go through a proxy or a DNS name that the consensus layer repoints. And I'd set synchronous replication to at least one replica, so a write isn't acknowledged until it's on two nodes.

Split brain is exactly what the consensus layer prevents. A node only acts as primary if it holds the lease from the quorum, so a partitioned old primary loses its lease and demotes itself or gets fenced. With two replicas plus the primary, quorum is three of four, so a minority partition can never elect a second primary.
